extracted.intended_audience: recent and soon-to-be PhDs (early-career political scientists and journal referees)
extracted.subtask_short: peer review for political science journals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guide for conducting and writing referee reports for academic journal submissions in political science, aimed at early-career scholars. Covers who journals invite as referees, what to include in a review, stylistic norms, timing, and how to calibrate recommendations to a journal's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to be invited as a referee
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals (e.g., International Organization, American Political Science Review) do not reach out to anyone without a PhD; each journal has its own policies and guidelines about whom they will invite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial staff build databases from graduate program websites, published work, and conferences. If you do not yet have a PhD you may still be invited by some journals, but others restrict invitations to those with completed doctorates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee panel expertise mix
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical review panel will include experts in the field, scholars with general knowledge of the field, and scholars with specific methodological and substantive expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors try to 'cover their bases' so that substantive, generalist, and methodological perspectives are represented. When papers are revised editors often re-invite the same set of reviewers; for methodological innovations or acknowledged lack of expertise they may invite additional referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding conflicts of interest and removing biased reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors generally exclude discussants and chairs of panels where the paper was presented, scholars acknowledged by the author, and others the author identifies as biased; reviewers who feel they have a serious bias should turn down the invitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have only a slight bias, explicitly acknowledge it to the editor (in the review or a note to the editor). Serious conflicts should prompt declining the review so editors can invite an impartial referee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose limits of your expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should explicitly note those cases/issues where they do not have deep expertise so that editors can assess the review fairly and, where necessary, invite additional referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State areas of weak expertise either within the report or in a private note to the editor (for example, if you lack technical knowledge of a particular method). This helps editors interpret recommendations and decide whether further expert review is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a clear, succinct argument for your recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: When you say there is a strong case for a particular recommendation make a succinct argument as to why; be explicit rather than relying on a long laundry list followed by a summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give two or three foundational points to support your recommendation. You need not be more definitive than you feel comfortable with, but do make your reasoning explicit so editors can act on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess suitability for the journal's audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the manuscript is suitable for the audience of the specific journal to which it was submitted; a paper might be salvageable but not appropriate for that journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsuitable for the current journal, mention one or two alternative, more appropriate venues. Fit to audience is as important as absolute quality when advising editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for the 'angel in the marble' (core idea with promise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about whether there is something in the manuscript—the kernel of an idea—which with some work can be brought out ('the angel in the marble').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you see a promising core, indicate how the authors might develop it; this helps editors and authors assess whether revision could produce a publishable paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a brief overview of where the manuscript fits in the literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an extremely brief overview to set the basis for your suggestions: is the contribution empirical, theoretical, or both, and what is the key value-added compared to previous work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may not know all the nuances of the literature; a short mapping of the manuscript's place helps both editors and authors. Avoid conflating novelty with quality and avoid dismissing revisiting prior ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish major deal-breaking reservations from minor quibbles
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear about the importance of different suggestions: which problems would sink the paper and which are minor issues that could be addressed without undermining the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark major vs minor issues explicitly. Examples: formatting/readability/typos are usually secondary; do not hold up a manuscript on a suggested extension unless it is central to the paper's claim. Raise non-essential missing citations toward the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't require extensions that are not central
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not hold a manuscript up with a suggested extension (e.g., further research or experiments) unless you see it as central to the contribution of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow authors to decide about extensions; recommend extensions only when they are necessary to substantiate the paper's main claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be succinct but thorough and well organized
rubrics_metrics.description: An average review should be a couple of pages long and organized (for example, distinguishing between theoretical and empirical issues, and major and minor suggestions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you think the paper is completely unsuitable for the specific journal, clearly specify why. Use headings or structure to make your review easy to parse for editors and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be courteous and gracious
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid snide comments; good scholarship is a process and reviewers should acknowledge the author's effort and highlight strengths even when recommending rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive tone preserves professional relationships and your own reputation; harsh or mean-spirited language is inappropriate in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific and avoid unsupported criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad generalizations (e.g., 'has no external validity' or 'literature review is incomplete') are unhelpful; take time to qualify and explain such statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples or evidence for criticisms so authors can address them. Remember you are not responsible for fixing the paper—your role is to diagnose and advise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be timely and communicate scheduling constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: If you know you will not be able to complete the review for several weeks, tell the editor; tardy reviewers are the single most important bottleneck in the publication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors typically expect reports within a month; long delays (e.g., three months overdue) significantly harm authors' careers. If you cannot meet deadlines, decline promptly or negotiate a realistic timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about accepting reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are under a time crunch, decline the review and, if possible, suggest one or two qualified alternatives; do not develop a habit of routinely declining reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering replacements helps editors and preserves goodwill. Repeatedly declining reduces future invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate the evolutionary nature of research and tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that tradeoffs often exist between theoretical/analytical strengths and empirical strengths; the scientific process is evolutionary and many good papers open debate rather than settle it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing tradeoffs, consider whether the paper contributes an important debate or opens a useful line of inquiry, even if not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete journals' quantitative evaluation but prioritize written coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals frequently require quantitative assessments (importance, clarity, persuasiveness); these questions underscore parameters that should frame your review but the number itself is less important than your written justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover relevance, clarity, persuasiveness, originality, and writing in your narrative review rather than agonizing over whether something is a '3' or '4' on the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate standards using journal purpose and acceptance rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Visit the journal's website to learn about its purpose, audience, and acceptance rate; compare your review behavior to typical acceptance rates to calibrate whether you are too lenient or too strict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have rejected all papers from a journal that accepts ~50%, you may be too critical; if you accept many from a journal that publishes 10%, you may be too lenient. Knowing scope also helps authors choose venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear and consistent recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: The clear recommendation should usually be expressed by ticking a summary evaluation (e.g., 'Reject' or 'Minor Revision') and your written report should be consistent with that choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recommending 'Major Revision' when you really mean 'Reject' or vice versa; consistency between your summary checkbox and the tone/content of your report is key for editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main responsibility: advise editors about fit and scholarly merits (not to decide or fix)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your main responsibility is to give the journal's editorial staff advice about whether the manuscript should be published in that specific journal and why; the specific decision (accept/reject) is not yours to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a substantiated argument about scholarly merits while keeping in mind journal purpose and audience. Offer course-of-action suggestions if helpful, but recognize the final decision rests with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use other reviewers' reports to learn and calibrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals allow reviewers to see the other reviews of the same manuscript, which lets you assess your own review and compare assessments across referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing disagreement among reviewers can be instructive and help you calibrate judgment; it also demonstrates that even important manuscripts can be evaluated differently by experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer to be a reviewer appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: If interested in reviewing, you can volunteer by emailing a journal's managing editor; some journals proactively recruit reviewers based on publications or conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subfield journals may encourage self-nomination. If you want to review, feel free to contact journals directly but understand each journal's policies about whom they invite.
